extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers learning or applying inductive methods and causal inference
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and applying methods of induction (Agreement, Difference, Joint, deductive and experimental approaches) to discover causes, especially in cases of multiple or interacting causes. Emphasizes when each method is reliable, its limitations, and practical steps (variation, negative instances, experiments) to strengthen inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: One effect may have several independent modes of production; a given effect can be produced by different causes or assemblages of conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the possibility of multiple causes renders simple Agreement uncertain: an observed antecedent A that co-occurs with effect a in two cases may not be the cause if different causes (e.g., C and E) produced a in each. Treat plurality as a central complication to be disproved or accommodated when inferring causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of the Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement (comparing cases that share a circumstance A leading to effect a) is uncertain when plurality of causes is possible; with few instances it yields only slight probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Agreement primarily to generate hypotheses/suggestions, not confirmations. Unless instances are very numerous and varied (eliminating other possible antecedents), Agreement alone is unreliable. Follow up Agreement findings with experiments or Method of Difference whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of the Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Difference (comparing a case where A B C → a b c with one where B C → b c so that adding A produces a) can establish that A was the cause or an indispensable portion of the cause in that instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two instances — a positive and a negative differing only by A — are sufficient for rigorous induction regarding that cause in those conditions. Prefer the Method of Difference when feasible, because it is not vitiated by plurality of causes in the same way as Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine positive instances that agree only in containing A with negative instances that agree only in not containing A; if so, A must be the only possible cause of a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This joint method avoids the characteristic imperfection of Agreement. It is especially powerful in observational sciences where direct experimentation is limited. Seek both premises (affirmative and negative) to secure causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Negative Instances in Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the Method of Agreement to negative instances (cases where phenomenon does not occur) is free from the characteristic imperfection affecting affirmative Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although theoretically powerful, negative-instance Agreement is often impractical because exhausting the field of negation is usually much harder than surveying positive cases (e.g., enumerating all non-transparent substances). Use when the negative field is tractable; otherwise rely on joint methods or experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Varying and Multiplying Instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing the number and, crucially, the variety of instances that all contain A strengthens the presumption that A is causally connected with a (unless plurality of causes persists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat observations across many unlike circumstances that share only A; with each diverse instance that still yields a, the hypothesis that A causes a is strengthened. Also attempt to exclude A in some combinations and test those (Method of Difference) to confirm causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Reliance on Mere Number of Instances
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere mass or number of similar instances adds nothing to evidence unless the added instances exclude additional antecedents; repeating identical-type instances is largely useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating quantity with quality of evidence. Prioritize analysis of what each instance eliminates; a single instance that excludes an antecedent can be more valuable than many repetitive ones. Before varying circumstances, repeat identical experiments only to check for error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Repetition to Exclude Error
rubrics_metrics.description: Before varying circumstances, it is necessary to repeat the same experiment/observation to assure oneself no error was made regarding individual observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrupulously repeat experiments without change until confident in the accuracy of the recorded facts; once assured, proceed to vary circumstances to test competing hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction as Primary Tool for Intermixture of Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes interfere or effects intermix (composition of causes), the instrument of Deduction alone is adequate to unravel complexities that inductive methods struggle with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deductive (a priori) reasoning from known laws of separate causes to derive the law of the combined effect. Inductive methods mainly supply premises and verification for such deductions; complex interferences often require theoretical/deductive treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Transformation and Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformation: two phenomena may be reciprocally cause and effect and each reproduce the other (e.g., water ⇄ hydrogen + oxygen). Composition: separate causes continue to produce their own effects which combine/merge and may obscure detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transformation occurs, the cause may be discovered among the effects and probed experimentally (chemical analysis). When composition occurs (effects co-exist and mask one another), direct induction is often inadequate and different approaches (deduction, synthetic study of simple elements) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical Analysis as Searching for Causes among Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where a new phenomenon reproduces its agents under certain conditions (e.g., water yielding hydrogen and oxygen), we can search for causes among the phenomenon's effects via analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit situations where the compound reproduces constituents experimentally; such cases are amenable to direct experiment and can reveal causal composition otherwise inaccessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes: express laws as tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because causes may be counteracted by others, laws of causation should be expressed as tendencies (e.g., body 'tends' to move under a force) rather than absolute statements that a result will always occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase general causal laws affirmatively of tendencies, or qualify them ('unless prevented' or 'except in so far as prevented'), to avoid apparent exceptions. Use domain-specific terms that capture tendency (e.g., 'pressure' in mechanics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of Simple Observation in Multifactorial Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of simple observation (comparing recoveries with or without a medicament) is inapplicable to complex effects dependent on many concurring causes (e.g., recovery from disease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect only vague impressions from mere observational correlation due to plurality of causes; small observed differences (more recoveries when mercury used) are of secondary practical value and nearly worthless for theory without experimental or deductive confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A posteriori experimental approach for composite causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental branch of a posteriori methods operates by manipulating causes and trying different combinations to observe their total effect (e.g., administering mercury in various circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach directly addresses causes rather than effects and may reveal the combination producing the composite phenomenon; however, complexity and many interacting factors can limit its success and require careful design and many controlled variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori (deductive) approach for composite causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductive (a priori) method derives the law of a composite effect from the known laws of the separate causes and known properties of the system (e.g., known properties of mercury and human body to infer therapeutic effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor a priori reasoning when reliable knowledge of component laws exists and when direct experimentation is impractical or unable to isolate contributions of each cause. Use deduction to predict conditions under which the combined law will yield the observed effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting plurality by failure to find common antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: When collating many instances of an effect, if no single antecedent is present in all of them but one or other of several antecedents always is, this indicates plurality of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze instance sets: inability to find a universal common antecedent suggests multiple sufficient causes; attempt to detect common elements among alternative antecedents to see if a deeper common cause exists; otherwise treat the different antecedents provisonally as distinct causes.
